progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m6-c13 (indicator as a weak acid HIn whose two forms differ in colour; the colour change as a reversible equilibrium shifted by acid and base; transition ranges; choose an indicator whose change falls inside the jump). chem-m6-c02 (properties of acids and bases; litmus). chem-m6-p03 (a calibrated pH meter; buffers as solutions that hold a known pH; colour judgements on indicator paper vary). chem-m6-c11 (buffers, by name). chem-m5-p01 (validity, reliability and accuracy in plain words; variables; risk assessment as hazard, harm, control). Stage 5 (the pH scale; universal indicator). Year 11 Biology is not assumed: "membranes" is said with its plain meaning ("the membranes in the cabbage cells, the thin layers that hold the pigment in") and shown on screen as a cell outline holding an internal pigment compartment, whose membranes break, so the cell wall is not mistaken for the barrier.
progression.startsWith: Prepare or select an indicator and record its initial colour. The video opens: Here's a beaker of purple juice from a red cabbage. Add a few drops of acid, and it turns red. Add a base, and it turns green.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining where the extract's colour comes from; preparing the extract and justifying each step; recording its starting colour; calibrating it against solutions of known pH with equal drops; reading its colour chart and stating its limits; using a water control; carrying out and explaining the reversibility cycle in one sample; recognising a colour change that is not reversible; estimating a pH from the chart and checking it with a meter; explaining why the extract is a poor titration indicator; naming the variables; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing the risk rows. No titration curves (chem-m6-c14), no anthocyanin structures, no meter calibration (chem-m6-p03).
progression.nextLesson: what a whole titration curve and a conductivity graph can tell you (route chem-m6-c14).

teaching.task: Purple juice from a red cabbage turns red in acid, green in base, and red again. How do you prepare it as an indicator, give each colour a meaning, and show that its colour change is a reversible reaction?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) one purple extract goes red, green and red again: can a vegetable work as an indicator, and how do you show the change runs both ways? (1); (2) the colour comes from anthocyanins; each behaves like the weak-acid indicator HIn from C13, but can lose more than one proton, and the extract is a mix of several of them, so it passes through several colours that blend gradually (2); (3) heat damages the membranes in the cabbage cells, the thin layers that hold the pigment in, so the pigment leaks out faster, and the pigment dissolves in water; filtering removes the solids so you see the solution's colour; the extract is cooled before use; its starting colour is recorded (3); (4) the colours mean nothing until they are matched to known pH; equal drops of extract in every well, because colour depth depends on how much pigment is present and you are comparing colour (4); (5) the chart shows several gradual changes; its precision is set by the spacing of the reference solutions (5); (6) adding any liquid dilutes the pigment, so the colour pales; the water well shows that paler purple, so a red or green well comes from the acid or base, not dilution; well C is read straight away (6); (7) one sample cycled: added base removes hydronium, so the pigment's equilibrium shifts to the forms that have lost protons, and acid shifts it back (C13 callback, one clause); three cycles in the same tube (7); (8) fresh wells show each colour separately, but only one sample going back and forth shows the reaction runs both ways; three cycles guard against a misread; the sample pales because it is diluted, but the same two colours return, which is evidence the pigment is not used up (8); (9) a colour that does not return is a warning: in strong base, like well C, for a long time the pigment molecules can change shape and break down (a different reaction), so base is added only until green and the cycle is run straight away (9); (10) the chart estimates household pH within a range, checked with a meter; the extract changes gradually, in steps, across the scale, while a titration needs one sharp change inside the jump (C13 callback), so it is a poor endpoint indicator (10); (11) variables; validity, reliability, accuracy (11); (12) the real hazards and controls (12); memory aid (13); attempts and brief feedback (14 to 17); decision rule and handoff (18); key notes (19).
teaching.conversationalApproach: purple red cabbage juice turns red in acid, green in base and red again, so the practical asks how to prepare it as an indicator, give each colour a meaning and show that its colour change is a reversible reaction. The colour is traced to anthocyanins that behave like HIn from the indicator video; the extract is prepared by the teacher in hot water (heat opens the cells), filtered and cooled; equal drops in wells of known pH give the colour chart; a water well is the control that shows dilution alone only makes the purple paler; one sample is cycled from acid to base and back three times, because fresh wells only show each colour separately; a colour that does not come back after a long time in strong base is a warning that the pigment has broken down. The chart is then used on vinegar and an ammonia cleaner, with its two-unit steps as its limit, followed by the variables, validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk assessment. The memory aid is "Steep. Chart. Cycle." Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Here's a beaker of purple juice from a red cabbage. Add a few drops of acid, and it turns red. Add a base, and it turns green. Add acid again, and the red comes back. So can you make a working indicator from a vegetable? And how would you show that its colour change really runs both ways?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A student adds 3 drops of red cabbage extract to each of three wells. Well A contains dilute hydrochloric acid, well B contains distilled water and well C contains dilute sodium hydroxide solution. Well A turns red, well B stays purple but is slightly paler than the extract, and well C turns green. (a) Explain why the student included well B. (b) Describe a test the student could carry out to show that the colour change of the extract is reversible." Answer: (a) well B is the control: it shows that adding liquid alone only dilutes the purple, so the red and green come from the acid and the base; (b) in one sample, add sodium hydroxide dropwise until green, then hydrochloric acid until red, and repeat the cycle three times; the same two colours returning shows the change runs both ways. Crossed mistake: "test the acid and the base again in fresh wells" (fresh wells show each colour, not a reversal). (A2) "A student made a colour chart for her red cabbage extract using buffer solutions: pH 2 red, pH 4 pink, pH 6 violet, pH 7 purple, pH 8 blue, pH 10 blue-green, pH 12 green. Three drops of the extract turned a solution of baking soda blue, with a slight green tint. (a) Estimate the pH of the baking soda solution. (b) Assess the accuracy of this method compared with a calibrated pH meter." Answer: (a) between 8 and 10, closer to 8: about 8 to 9; (b) less accurate: the chart steps are up to two units wide, the change between them is gradual, and colour is judged by eye, so it gives a range, while a calibrated meter is accurate to within a few hundredths. Crossed mistake: "pH = 8.0" (false precision: a colour match gives a range).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct an investigation to demonstrate the preparation and use of indicators as illustrators of the characteristics and properties of acids and bases and their reversible reactions (ACSCH101)" this video prepares students to carry out and analyse the natural indicator practical; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: what gives red cabbage its colour (a mixture of anthocyanin pigments that behave like C13's weak-acid indicator, each with more than one proton to lose, so several gradual colours); preparing the extract (chop, steep in hot water, filter, cool) and why each step matters; recording the starting colour; calibrating the extract against solutions of known pH with equal drops on a white tile, and why the drops must be equal; reading the colour chart and why its precision depends on the spacing of the reference solutions; the water control, which separates dilution from a pH effect; the reversibility test (one sample cycled acid, base, acid, three times) and why it must be the same sample; what a colour that does not return means (the pigment changing shape and breaking down, a different reaction); using the chart to estimate the pH of household samples and checking with a meter; why a natural extract is a poor titration indicator; variables; validity, reliability and accuracy; the risk assessment. Not re-taught (chem-m6-c13, recalled in one clause each): an indicator as a weak acid HIn whose two forms differ in colour; the colour change as an equilibrium shifted by added acid or base (Le Chatelier); transition ranges; choosing an indicator that changes inside the jump. Not here: titration curves and conductivity graphs (chem-m6-c14, the next video); the chemistry of individual anthocyanin forms (author note b); calibrating a pH meter (chem-m6-p03, recalled); how buffers work (chem-m6-c11; named here as "solutions that hold a known pH", as in P03); calculating a concentration from a colour (colour is categorical; plan note kept).

Colour key on screen throughout (C01, C13): hydronium teal, hydroxide violet; acid bottles carry a teal tab, base bottles a violet tab, water grey; the extract's colours as coded swatches matched to the painted plates; controls green, hazards terracotta. Board layout (three zones, constant): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the plates (beaker, well plate, filter); the right third holds the current card (method step, colour chart, VRA, risk table), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends.
